why: Rung 1's 'officially approved imports of H200 chips by at least one Chinese firm' is met by Alibaba's October 2026 approval, and rung 2 holds 'only when rung 1 does not', so ByteDance's refusal does not count.
No firm is approved, and one firm's withdrawal with two requests still under review is neither a 'refusal of the requests' nor a 'withdrawal of it as a whole', so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.
'An official Chinese refusal of the requests ... or a prohibition of the imports, stands on 2027-01-31 with no firm approved' is exactly the November refusal of every request, unchanged since.

With no firm approved, every firm withdrawing its request so that none is left reads as 'a formal abandonment or withdrawal of it as a whole' standing on the due day (and the domestic-chip rule as an 'other decision against the event of rung 1'), though the rung's 'it' is the approval while what was withdrawn are the requests.

Rung 1 asks only that the authorities 'have officially approved' a firm's imports 'on or before 2027-01-31', which the October approval satisfies; it does not say the approval must still stand, and rung 2 holds 'only when rung 1 does not'.
With no approval and no official refusal, prohibition or other decision of any kind, 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.

A licensing rule published in the Federal Register in November 2026 is the department having 'adopted ... a licensing rule ... on advanced AI-chip shipments to third countries' on or before the due day.

Nothing has been 'adopted', and withdrawing one proposal while another is open for comment is neither an announcement that it 'will adopt no such restriction' nor a withdrawal 'as a whole', so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.

The November announcement that it will not go beyond the May guidance is 'an announcement by the Commerce Department that it will adopt no such restriction', and it 'stands on 2027-01-31' with nothing adopted.

Rung 1 asks only that the department 'has adopted a binding restriction, a licensing rule or any other' on or before the due day, which the September adoption satisfies whatever the later rescission, and rung 2 holds 'only when rung 1 does not'.
Nothing was 'adopted' and there is no announcement or decision against it, so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.
No sale is shown, and the prohibition was lifted in December so it no longer 'stands on 2027-01-31', which leaves 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.
'A formal Chinese prohibition on purchases of H200 chips ... stands on 2027-01-31' because it is in force on the due day, an announced review not having lifted it, and no sale has been made.
The November 2026 Form 10-Q is one of 'Nvidia's disclosures ... published on or before that day' showing that Nvidia 'has made H200 sales' to a customer in China.
No sale is 'shown by Nvidia's disclosures or by official Chinese statements', and a permission is no 'prohibition' or 'decision against the event', so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.
The deal closing in June 2027 is Nvidia having 'completed the acquisition of Hugging Face on or before 2028-03-05', and the renegotiated price touches nothing in the rung.

Both companies confirming they will not go on after the agreement expired is 'a termination of the acquisition announced by Nvidia or Hugging Face' (a 'formal abandonment ... of it as a whole') that stands on the due day.
A regulator suing to block is not yet 'a regulator's block of it' that 'stands', the deal is not 'completed' and neither company has announced a 'termination', so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.

The court's December 2027 block is an 'other decision against the event of rung 1 as a whole' that still 'stands on 2028-03-05', since the pending appeal has not overturned it, and the deal is not completed.
The deal is not 'completed', and moving the latest closing date is no 'termination', 'block' or 'abandonment', so 'neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds'.
